items.en: Why "Uncontaminated" Isn't Enough for the Highest Dharmas
parent: V. Discriminating the Dharma and Mind of Dhyāna-Pāramitā

zh: 問曰：何故言法華三昧等法皆名非有漏非無漏？如《法華》中說：「是德藏菩薩於無漏實相心已得通達，其次當作佛，號曰為淨身。」又如四無畏中，第二無畏名無漏無畏。如是等法，諸經論中多悉說為無漏，今何以言皆是非有漏非無漏法？答曰：此欲簡諸佛菩薩有中道不共之法，故須作此分別。如凡夫專依有漏，二乘偏行無漏。今諸佛菩薩所得不共之法，不滯二邊，則無二邊之漏失，是以悉云無漏。何故得免二邊漏失？正以中道之法非二邊所攝，故云非有漏非無漏也。此之二說，語異而意同，故無乖失。
en: Question: Why is it said that the Lotus samādhi and dharmas like it are all called "neither contaminated nor uncontaminated"? As the Lotus Sūtra itself says: "This Bodhisattva Store of Virtue has already penetrated the mind of the uncontaminated true reality; next he shall become a buddha, named Pure Body." And likewise, among the four kinds of fearlessness, the second is called "the fearlessness of the uncontaminated." Dharmas of this kind are, in most sūtras and treatises, spoken of simply as uncontaminated — why, then, is it now said that they are all "neither contaminated nor uncontaminated"?

Answer: This is meant to set apart the unshared dharma of the middle way possessed by the buddhas and bodhisattvas, and so this distinction must be made. Just as ordinary people rely exclusively on the contaminated, and the two lesser vehicles practice one-sidedly in the uncontaminated — the unshared dharma attained by the buddhas and bodhisattvas does not become fixed in either extreme, and so has no leakage into either extreme, and is therefore, in every case, called "uncontaminated." How is leakage into either extreme avoided? Precisely because the dharma of the middle way is not contained within either extreme — hence it is called "neither contaminated nor uncontaminated." These two ways of putting it differ in wording but agree in meaning, and so there is no contradiction between them.

zh: 若任理性而論，則一切皆名非有漏非無漏法，故《大品經》云：「色無縛無脫，乃至一切種智無縛無脫。」理既無縛無脫，稱理之行豈不同名無縛無脫？無縛無脫者，即是非有漏非無漏之異名也。問曰：分別定慧為四句可爾，戒復云何？答曰：從十善、三歸、五戒、八齋戒、沙彌十戒、大比丘二百五十戒、菩薩十重四十八輕戒，亦得作四句分別其義（云云），今不具釋。問曰：上第四、明禪詮次及下第七、辨修證中，皆先明有漏，次亦有漏亦無漏，次無漏，次非有漏非無漏。今分別四句法，何故異於前後，乃以三為二也？答曰：前後皆約修行入證以為詮次。今欲簡別法心之相事，須約言句為便。亦以諸經論中說四句皆爾，故云行時非說時，說時非行時，此義易明。
en: If one argues purely in terms of principle, then everything whatsoever may be called "neither contaminated nor uncontaminated" — hence the Larger Sūtra says: "Form has no bondage and no liberation, and so on up through the wisdom that knows all things in every mode, which likewise has no bondage and no liberation." Since principle itself has no bondage and no liberation, how could conduct that accords with principle not equally be called "without bondage, without liberation"? "Without bondage, without liberation" is simply another name for "neither contaminated nor uncontaminated."

Question: Sorting concentration and wisdom into this fourfold scheme is understandable enough — but what of precepts? Answer: From the ten wholesome deeds, the three refuges, the five precepts, the eight precepts of the fast-day, the śrāmaṇera's ten precepts, the full monk's two hundred and fifty precepts, and the bodhisattva's ten major and forty-eight minor precepts — these too can be sorted into this same fourfold scheme (and so on), though the full explanation will not be given here.

Question: Above, in the fourth topic, and further below, in the seventh topic distinguishing cultivation and realization, both first clarify the contaminated, next both contaminated and uncontaminated, next the uncontaminated, and next neither contaminated nor uncontaminated. Why, in sorting this fourfold scheme here, does the order differ, placing what was third now second? Answer: The order given before and after is arranged in terms of the sequence of cultivation entering realization. Here, in wishing to distinguish the mark of dharma and mind as a matter of exposition, the order is arranged for convenience of statement instead. This is likewise how the various sūtras and treatises state this fourfold scheme in general — hence it is said, "the time of practice is not the time of exposition, and the time of exposition is not the time of practice" — this point is easily understood.

The middle way is defined here by what it escapes rather than what it positively is: not "uncontaminated" in the ordinary sense (which still implies an opposition to "contaminated," and so still leans on one side of a pair), but a dharma that cannot leak into either side of any such pair to begin with. Pushed to its limit, this same reasoning — via the Larger Sūtra's "no bondage, no liberation" — threatens to erase the fourfold scheme altogether, since on that logic everything is ultimately "neither contaminated nor uncontaminated." Zhiyi doesn't shy from this. On the question of order, he notes that practice and exposition follow two different sequences: cultivation entering realization has its own order (contaminated, both, uncontaminated, neither), while exposition arranges the same four for convenience of statement — "the time of practice is not the time of exposition." The point is picked up again in the tetralemma discussion below.

items.en: Four Kinds of Mind, across Four Moments
parent: V. Discriminating the Dharma and Mind of Dhyāna-Pāramitā

zh: 第二、明心，有四種心：一、有漏心；二、無漏心；三、亦有漏亦無漏心；四、非有漏非無漏心。一、有漏心者，即是凡夫、外道心，具三漏故，名有漏心。所以者何？凡夫、外道修禪定時，約四時中分別，不得離結漏故。何等為四時中分別？一者、初發心欲修禪時，不能厭患世間，為求禪定中樂及果報故；二者、當修禪時，不能返照觀察，生見著心；三者、證諸禪時，即計為實，不知虛誑，於地地中見著心生；四者、從禪定起，若對眾境，還生結業，以是因緣，名為漏心。
en: Second, clarifying mind: mind is of four kinds — first, contaminated mind; second, uncontaminated mind; third, both contaminated and uncontaminated mind; fourth, neither contaminated nor uncontaminated mind.

First, contaminated mind: this is precisely the mind of the ordinary person and the non-Buddhist practitioner, complete with the three contaminants — hence it is called contaminated mind. Why is this? When ordinary people and non-Buddhist practitioners cultivate dhyāna-concentration, this can be distinguished across four moments, in none of which are they able to leave the fetters and contaminants behind. What are these four moments? First, at the very moment the mind first arises, wishing to cultivate dhyāna, they are unable to grow weary of the world, seeking instead the pleasure and the fruit found within dhyāna-concentration. Second, at the moment of actually cultivating it, they are unable to turn contemplation back upon themselves, and a mind of views and attachment arises. Third, at the moment of realizing the various dhyānas, they take them at once to be real, not knowing them to be illusory and deceptive, so that a mind of views and attachment arises at every single stage. Fourth, upon emerging from dhyāna-concentration, when facing the various objects of the world, the fetters and karma arise once again. For these reasons, this is called a contaminated mind.

zh: 第二、明無漏心，亦約四時中分別：一、約發心者，二乘之人初發心欲修禪時，厭患世間，不樂禪樂及求果報，但為調心，則漏心自然微薄不起，因此能發無漏；二、修行者隨所修禪，悉知虛假，能伏見著，不生結業；三、得證者入諸禪定之時，若於定中發真空慧，斷諸煩惱，則三漏永盡；四、從禪定起，隨所對境，不生見著，造諸結業，以是因緣，名無漏心。前二心雖是有漏，而為無漏作因，因中說果，亦名無漏。
en: Second, clarifying uncontaminated mind: this too is distinguished across four moments. First, as to the arising of the mind: when a follower of the two lesser vehicles first sets the mind on cultivating dhyāna, they grow weary of the world, taking no delight in the pleasure of dhyāna or in seeking its fruit, but cultivate only to tame the mind — the contaminated mind then naturally grows faint of itself and does not arise, and through this the uncontaminated can be brought forth. Second, as to practicing: whatever dhyāna is cultivated, it is entirely known to be illusory and unreal, so that views and attachment can be subdued, and fetters and karma do not arise. Third, as to attaining realization: at the moment of entering the various concentrations, if true wisdom of emptiness is brought forth within concentration, severing every affliction, then the three contaminants are forever exhausted. Fourth, upon emerging from dhyāna-concentration, whatever objects are faced, views and attachment do not arise, nor is any fettering karma produced. For these reasons, this is called uncontaminated mind. Though the first two moments are still, strictly speaking, contaminated, they serve as the cause of the uncontaminated — and since the fruit is spoken of within the cause, they too are called uncontaminated.

zh: 第三、明亦有漏亦無漏心，亦約四時中分別：一、約發心者，此行人初發心欲修禪時，恛惶不定，或時厭離生死，不樂禪樂；或生見著，悕望定樂，愛樂果報。以生厭故，結業微羸；悕望定樂故，增長煩惱。二、約修行者，如不斷善根人欲修禪時，是人雖成就信等五法，不得名根。以其不能定伏結使，故名亦有漏。生於信等善法，故名亦無漏。三、約得證者，七種學人入諸禪時，雖發真智，結漏未盡，故名亦有漏亦無漏，乃至退法羅漢亦有此義。所以者何？未得無生智，故名亦有漏；得盡智，故名亦無漏。四、諸學人等從禪定起，隨對眾境，隨所斷惑，未盡之處或猶生著，故名亦有漏；斷惑盡處雖對眾境，結業不起，名亦無漏。
en: Third, clarifying mind that is both contaminated and uncontaminated: this too is distinguished across four moments. First, as to the arising of the mind: when this kind of practitioner first sets the mind on cultivating dhyāna, they waver, unsettled — at times growing weary of birth-and-death, taking no delight in the pleasure of dhyāna; at other times giving rise to views and attachment, longing for the bliss of concentration and delighting in its fruit. Because weariness arises, fettering karma is somewhat weakened; but because longing for the bliss of concentration arises, affliction grows. Second, as to practicing: take, for instance, a person who has not severed their wholesome roots and wishes to cultivate dhyāna — though such a person has accomplished the five factors beginning with faith, these cannot yet be called "faculties," since they are unable to fix and subdue the fetters — hence this is called "also contaminated." Yet because faith and the other wholesome factors have arisen, it is also called "also uncontaminated." Third, as to attaining realization: when the seven kinds of trainee enter the various dhyānas, though true wisdom is brought forth, the fetters and contaminants are not yet exhausted — hence this is called both contaminated and uncontaminated; the same holds even for the arhat liable to regression. Why is this? Since the wisdom of no-arising is not yet attained, it is called "also contaminated"; since the wisdom of exhaustion is attained, it is called "also uncontaminated." Fourth, when these various trainees emerge from dhyāna-concentration and face the various objects of the world, wherever the delusion they are severing is not yet exhausted, attachment may still arise there — hence this is called "also contaminated"; but wherever the delusion is already exhausted, though objects are faced, fettering karma does not arise — hence this is called "also uncontaminated."

zh: 第四、釋非有漏非無漏心，亦約四時中明：一、約發心者，菩薩大士初發意欲修禪時，不為生死，不為涅槃，則心不墮二邊；二、約修行者，菩薩修禪波羅蜜時，為福德故，不住無為，為智慧故，不住有為；三、約得證者，菩薩入諸禪時，若於禪中發無生忍慧，爾時心與法性相應，不著生死，不染涅槃；四、菩薩從禪定起，隨對眾境，心常不依有無二邊，以是因緣，菩薩之心名非有漏非無漏心。
en: Fourth, explaining mind that is neither contaminated nor uncontaminated: this too is clarified across four moments. First, as to the arising of the mind: when a great bodhisattva first sets the intention to cultivate dhyāna, it is neither for the sake of birth-and-death nor for the sake of nirvāṇa — so the mind does not fall into either extreme. Second, as to practicing: when the bodhisattva cultivates dhyāna-pāramitā, for the sake of merit they do not abide in the unconditioned, and for the sake of wisdom they do not abide in the conditioned. Third, as to attaining realization: when the bodhisattva enters the various dhyānas, if the wisdom of the forbearance of no-arising is brought forth within dhyāna, then the mind, at that moment, is in accord with the dharma-nature — neither attached to birth-and-death nor defiled by nirvāṇa. Fourth, when the bodhisattva emerges from dhyāna-concentration and faces the various objects of the world, the mind never relies on either the extreme of existence or the extreme of nonexistence. For these reasons, the bodhisattva's mind is called neither contaminated nor uncontaminated mind.

The same fourfold grid now applies to the practicing subject rather than the object practiced, and Zhiyi runs each of the four kinds of mind through the identical four-moment template — arising, practicing, realizing, and emerging from concentration — which makes the four minds easy to compare side by side. Watch what changes across the row for "arising": ordinary craving for pleasure and result (contaminated), weariness of the world alone (uncontaminated), an unstable wavering between the two (both), and a motivation that simply never frames the question in terms of saṃsāra versus nirvāṇa at all (neither) — the bodhisattva's mind, from the very first moment, is not on the same axis the other three are measured against.

quiz.q: The sūtras usually call the Lotus samādhi and the like "uncontaminated," yet this treatise says "neither contaminated nor uncontaminated." How does the text reconcile them?
options: the two contradict each other but both stand
not stuck in either extreme, there is no leakage, hence "uncontaminated"; the middle way is not contained in either extreme, hence "neither"; the wording differs but the meaning agrees
quiz.why: "The unshared dharma attained by the buddhas and bodhisattvas does not become fixed in either extreme, and so has no leakage into either extreme, and is therefore, in every case, called 'uncontaminated' ... the dharma of the middle way is not contained within either extreme — hence it is called 'neither contaminated nor uncontaminated.' These two ways of putting it differ in wording but agree in meaning."

quiz.q: The fourth and seventh topics put "both" before "uncontaminated," but here the order is reversed. How does the text explain this?
options: before and after follow the order of practice entering realization; here the order suits exposition — the time of practice is not the time of exposition
in practice, too, the uncontaminated should come first
quiz.why: "The order given before and after is arranged in terms of the sequence of cultivation entering realization. Here, in wishing to distinguish the mark of dharma and mind as a matter of exposition, the order is arranged for convenience of statement instead ... the time of practice is not the time of exposition." It is neither an error nor a claim that the uncontaminated is shallower.

quiz.q: For the mind that is neither contaminated nor uncontaminated, "as to practicing," what is the bodhisattva's mind like?
options: wavering — sometimes weary of birth-and-death, sometimes longing for the bliss of concentration
for merit they do not abide in the unconditioned; for wisdom they do not abide in the conditioned
unable to turn contemplation back, giving rise to attachment
knowing every dhyāna to be unreal, subduing views and attachment
quiz.why: "When the bodhisattva cultivates dhyāna-pāramitā, for the sake of merit they do not abide in the unconditioned, and for the sake of wisdom they do not abide in the conditioned." Knowing dhyāna as unreal is the uncontaminated mind practicing, wavering is the "both" mind arising, and failing to turn back is the contaminated mind practicing.
